items.title: Chris Pappas holds New Hampshire US Senate seat for Democrats
items.content_html:
Nov 3 (Reuters) - Democrat Chris Pappas won New Hampshire's open US Senate seat on Tuesday, according to media projections, defeating Republican John Sununu and preserving a crucial Democratic seat as the party fights to take control of the chamber.

Pappas' victory denied Republicans a pickup in the cold-weather state, where high energy prices had become a major issue amid President Donald Trump's war with Iran. He will succeed Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, who is retiring after 18 years.

Pappas, a moderate US House member, blamed Trump and fellow Republicans for the Iran war, which has disrupted oil shipments and driven up gasoline and heating oil prices.

Sununu, a former US senator from a prominent New Hampshire political family, argued that increased domestic energy production would lower prices.

Republicans held a 53-47 Senate majority going into Tuesday's elections, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.

New Hampshire has long been considered a swing state because of its moderate electorate, and Republicans had targeted Shaheen's seat in their drive to retain their Senate majority.

Reporting by Richard Cowan; Editing by Howard Goller

items.title: Senator Jon Ossoff wins reelection, holding Georgia for Democrats
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won reelection in Georgia on Tuesday, according to media projections, defeating President Donald Trump-backed Republican US Representative Mike Collins and preserving a crucial seat in his party's battle for Senate control.

Ossoff triumphed in one of the nation's most competitive Senate races in a state Trump carried by 2 percentage points in 2024, underscoring Democrats' ability to defend a key battleground.

Ossoff, widely seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, raised $126 million more than Collins, who was backed by $18 million in outside spending after fighting through a three-way Republican primary and runoff.

Trump endorsed Collins over former college football coach Derek Dooley, who was backed by outgoing Republican Governor Brian Kemp.

Republicans held a 53-47 Senate majority going into Tuesday's elections, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.

Democrats' easiest path to a Senate majority requires the party to hold seats in Trump-won Georgia and Michigan and flip Republican-held seats in Maine and North Carolina, as well as at least two other states that Trump won by double digits in 2024, such as Ohio, Alaska, Iowa, Texas and others.

Reporting by Nolan D. McCaskill; Editing by Michael Learmonth and Howard Goller

items.title: 'It is a cappuccino. It can't be $10,' says Harry Styles about NYC coffee prices
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Singer Harry Styles, who recently completed a 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden in New York, thought prices for coffee in the city were some of the spookiest things he saw around Halloween.

"It is a cappuccino. It can't be $10, it can't be," he said during one of his last concerts, according to videos posted by fans on social media.

"The scariest thing about this Halloween is the price of caffeinated beverages in this city. Astronomical. It's out of control," he added, before also complaining about expensive tipping.

Some fans, in comments after the video, thought it was amusing that such a wealthy and successful personality would complain about such an ordinary thing as the price for a cup of coffee.

"Harry is right... $10 for a cappuccino plus at least a 20% tip?," said one fan. "Are you for real?"

Others, meanwhile, criticized ticket prices for his concerts.

Coffee has suffered a series of cost shocks in recent years including climate-related production shortfalls in major producers and the imposition of US tariffs, which were later removed.

The price of a pound of ground roast coffee in US cities averaged $9.33 in September, according to the latest inflation reading from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

That is the highest ever for the month and 91% higher than in 2020, adding another item to the cost of living discussion as the US votes in the midterm elections.

Coffee companies say they had to cut profit margins during the cost shock to prevent prices rising even more, and are now in a period of recovering their margins.

Reporting by Marcelo Teixeira; editing by Lincoln Feast.

items.title: US moves to drop smuggling charges against Harvard scientist
items.content_html:
BOSTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - US prosecutors moved on Tuesday to drop criminal charges against a Russian-born scientist at Harvard University accused of smuggling frog embryos into the United States after she argued the Trump administration had singled her out for prosecution.

Federal prosecutors in Boston said in a court filing they were dismissing the charges against Kseniia Petrova after a federal judge cleared the way for her to obtain evidence supporting her claim that she was being vindictively prosecuted.

Prosecutors in the filing said that while they viewed those claims as "meritless," continuing to prosecute the case after the judge's order "would divert significant time and attention from more substantial federal interests."

A spokesperson for US Attorney Leah Foley, the Trump administration's top federal prosecutor in Massachusetts, declined to comment.

A lawyer for Petrova had no immediate comment.

The biomedical researcher had been taken into custody by US immigration authorities at the airport in Boston in February 2025 after her visa was revoked upon her return from a trip to France.

Prosecutors brought a criminal case against Petrova, who worked at Harvard Medical School, in May 2025 as a federal judge in Vermont weighed ordering her release from the immigration detention facility in Louisiana.

Prosecutors alleged that US Customs and Border Protection agents stopped Petrova after her checked duffel bag was flagged for inspection, revealing the frog embryos that they said should have been declared to customs officials.

Petrova, who was ultimately released on bail in June 2025, pleaded not guilty to the smuggling and false statement charges she faced. She has said her boss asked her to bring back frog embryo samples for experiments.

Her lawyers argued the charges were brought in retaliation for her decision to challenge the immigration proceedings against her and said that the case had been brought amid a broader campaign by President Donald Trump's administration against researchers, universities and Harvard itself.

In April, a federal judge in Vermont ruled that Petrova's visa had been unlawfully canceled. And last month, a judge in Boston concluded she put forward sufficient evidence that she was selectively prosecuted to entitle her to obtain access to government records to support her claim.

“We seem to be getting everything we want,” Trump said in the six-minute telephone interview.

items.title: Trump says US close to trade deal with Canada, Carney says work remains
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Tuesday the United States was close to making a trade deal with Canada, but Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said work remained to be done and that Washington had dropped some demands.

"Canada is very good, we're going to make a deal with Canada very soon. We're going to make a great deal," Trump said in an interview with Fox News.

Canada and the United States have slapped billions of dollars in tariffs on each other in recent months. The imposition of tariffs on Canada has emerged as an issue in some northern US border states like Michigan and Maine ahead of Tuesday's US midterm elections.

Trump and Carney said on Sunday they had spoken about a trade deal.

Carney said the US had withdrawn some earlier demands, including one that would have given Washington final say over any trade deals that Canada might seek to sign with other nations.

"We've made progress, but we haven't finished. You know, if I were to paraphrase it, it's they're asking less and they're offering more, but we're not quite there," he told a televised news conference at the end of a summit in Antigua.

Reporting by Humeyra Pamuk, Doina Chiacu and Susan Heavey in Washington and Dadvid Ljunggren in Ottawa; Editing by Michelle Nichols and Jonathan Spicer

items.title: Triumphal Arch would not be completed until Trump leaves office, DOJ says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department said on Tuesday that President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot (76-meter) triumphal arch in Washington would not be completed until after the end of his second term.

If it is given the go-ahead, the DOJ said it expects an initial six to eight months of construction focused on excavation and foundation work that could begin as soon as Thursday, with above-ground construction beginning in May 2027 at the earliest. Total construction is anticipated to take 33 to 39 months, the government said.

The project, modeled on Paris' Arc de Triomphe, is planned for near Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia, just across the Potomac River from Washington.

The National Capital Planning Commission is set to hold a meeting to approve the project on Thursday and the Department of the Interior said in a court filing it may issue a final decision to approve the proposal the same day. The National Park Service may also issue a permit or other authorization on Thursday, the department added.

But the arch has faced significant opposition in the courts. The state of Virginia and the District of Columbia sued the National Park Service and Department of the Interior on Saturday, seeking to halt the start of construction, calling it "legally indefensible" and arguing Congress has not approved it.

Several veterans have also sued to block the arch, arguing it would destroy the historic sightline between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

The government urged US Judge Tanya Chutkan in the District of Columbia to reject the effort to stop construction. It argued that the arch's location and height could be used to defend the capital from evolving threats such as drones.

Others have raised fears about the arch's proximity to Reagan Washington National Airport and location within the airport's main approach and departure corridors.

But the Federal Aviation Administration found the arch did not pose aviation safety risks. The FAA said the arch will include an eternal flame and floodlight projectors pointed at it to make it noticeable for pilots.

The arch is part of Trump's broader push to remake Washington, including renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, redeveloping a golf course in East Potomac Park, adding his name to the US Institute of Peace, and attempting to add his name to the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

items.title: Nine things on US voters' minds ahead of midterm elections, according to Reuters/Ipsos poll
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, November 3 - The rising cost of living will be top of mind for Americans as they head to the polls in Tuesday's midterm elections which will determine control of Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's term.

What follows are results from a Reuters/Ipsos poll of 1,765 US adults conducted nationwide Thursday through Monday — making the survey distinct from an exit poll which includes voters surveyed as they leave polling stations. The poll had a margin of error of 3 percentage points for registered voters.

THE COST OF LIVING

Some 48% of registered voters in the poll say the cost of living is the top issue for deciding how they will vote, compared with 26% who say democratic norms and 13% who point to immigration. US fuel prices have surged since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in February.

DONALD TRUMP

Trump has urged supporters to pretend he is on the ballot in an effort to energize his Republican Party. The Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that 48% of people who planned to vote — or already had done so — said they thought of their ballots as a vote against Trump, compared to 25% who said they were voting for him. Some 25% said Trump was not a factor in their vote.

IRAN

Trump has argued that war was necessary to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons. Some 25% of voters think military action has been worth the cost, and 55% say it has not been worth it. Some 18% weren't sure.

ELECTION INTEGRITY

Voters overall trust the US electoral process, with 77% saying they are confident their ballots will be counted but 45% saying they think voter fraud is a widespread problem. Trump has falsely claimed that massive numbers of non-citizens vote illegally and election officials worry the administration could disrupt the election or certification of results it views unfavorably. The White House says its goal is to safeguard election integrity and voting security.

HOUSEHOLD FINANCES

Some 49% of Americans think their household finances have gotten worse since January 2025, when Trump returned to power, compared with 13% who said their finances have gotten better and 37% who say things are about the same. Trump campaigned ahead of the November 2024 presidential election with a promise to turbocharge the economy, but his presidential approval has fallen in recent months to the lowest levels of his political career, including among Hispanic Americans who swung in his direction in 2024. The latest poll showed 54% of Hispanics said their household finances have suffered, while 10% said they had improved.

TRANSGENDER SPORTS

Some 38% of voters ahead of the election said keeping transgender girls and women out of women's sports was a very important issue or the most important issue, compared to 25% who said that about protecting the rights of transgender people.

DATA CENTERS

Some 42% of registered voters in the poll said limiting the construction of data centers used to power AI was very important or the most important issue.

MEGA DONORS

The ultra-rich face few limits on how much they can spend to influence federal elections. A bipartisan majority of registered voters — including 93% of Democrats and 71% of Republicans — think it is inappropriate for billionaires to contribute tens of millions of dollars to influence elections.

POLITICAL OPTIONS

While poll respondents appeared to narrowly favor Democrats over Republicans for this year's congressional elections, they remain divided on which party has good ideas. Some 43% of registered voters in the poll said Democrats had at least some good ideas, while 39% said the same of Republicans.

Reporting by Jason Lange in Washington; editing by Scott Malone and Rod Nickel

items.title: Democrat Ossoff wins Georgia Senate race as US midterm elections enter final hours
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Polls closed in more than half of US states on Tuesday evening, as Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won the first major race call of midterm elections that will decide whether Democrats can wrest control of Congress from President Donald Trump's Republicans.

Ossoff, widely seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, defeated US Representative Mike Collins, media outlets projected, in a contest that was once considered competitive but moved out of reach for Republicans amid Trump's declining approval ratings.

As of 8 p.m. ET (0100 GMT), US media had projected winners in roughly three dozen House and Senate races, though none was among the contests expected to be decisive in determining control of either chamber. Democrats need to net three House seats and four Senate seats to win majorities.

According to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets including major television networks and the Associated Press, half of voters nationwide said they saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president, and three-quarters said they are "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the way the country is headed.

In addition, 70% of voters surveyed said they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president.

Democrats were favored to win the House, while the Senate battle was unfolding across several closely contested states, as millions of Americans cast ballots in an election that served as a referendum on the first two years of Trump's second term. Trump himself told his supporters to "pretend I'm on the ballot."

History is against Republicans: The sitting president's party has lost ground in Congress in all but two midterms since World War Two. Trump's approval rating is hovering near his career lows, with voters frustrated by war with Iran, higher fuel prices and wider affordability concerns.

Led by Trump, Republicans have portrayed Democratic candidates as radical, un-American and even communist, labels Democrats flatly reject.

The president has sought to energize his base with more than two dozen campaign rallies since the start of October, most in states he easily won in 2024, underscoring Republicans' defensive posture.

Opinion polls show voters are most concerned about affordability and disapprove of Trump's handling of the issue. His tariffs on imports, many of which the courts threw out, and his decision to attack Iran in February raised prices for consumers.

TRUMP DEPLOYS ELECTION MONITORS

There are 47 US House races widely seen as competitive, according to a Reuters analysis of the leading election forecasters. If the other contests all proceed as predicted, Democrats would need to win only 13 of those races to secure a majority.

But Democrats have little margin for error in the Senate. The party must defend all of its current seats while winning at least two states that voted for Trump by a double-digit margin two years ago, such as Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas.

Opinion polls show Democrats either narrowly leading or within striking distance in all of those states.

Legal observers and Democrats have warned that Trump, who has long falsely claimed that US elections are rigged, may attempt to challenge Tuesday's results if Republicans lose.

The US Justice Department said it had deployed 1,000 election monitors and observers to all 50 states in what it called the largest Election Day monitoring effort in history.

Democrats criticized the plan as potential voter intimidation. In roughly two-thirds of the jurisdictions the department listed, voters supported Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump in the 2024 presidential election, a Reuters analysis found.

ELECTION INTRIGUE IN ALASKA

A New York Times report upended the Alaska Senate race when it reported that the campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, 53, helped recruit a third candidate to run as an independent who shares the first and last name of her Republican opponent, Dan Sullivan, 61.

Peltola has denied involvement. Trump's Justice Department has launched a criminal probe into the allegations and filed a lawsuit to block certification of the election results, though a judge dismissed the latter effort.

Supporters of the incumbent Sullivan said they were not confused by the presence of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot.

"They make it pretty obvious: It says 'incumbent' after his name," said Jake Wesley, 27, who grew up in Anchorage and is now stationed there in the US Air Force. In recent days, Trump has complained repeatedly that voters may not know the meaning of the word.

items.title: Six things to watch as US voters decide control of Congress
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, November 2 - Americans head to the polls on Tuesday in midterm elections that will decide control of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term.

The results will serve as the first nationwide verdict on Trump's presidency, revealing whether voters want to check the Republican president's power by giving Democrats control of one or both chambers of Congress or are willing to accept the status quo despite frustrations over the cost of living and the US-led war with Iran.

The outcome could also reshape debates within both parties over which messages and policies resonate most with voters ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

Here are six things to watch on Election Day.

THE RACES THAT WILL DECIDE CONTROL OF CONGRESS

Democrats need a net gain of four seats in both the US House of Representatives and US Senate to overturn Republicans' narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities.

They are widely expected to reclaim the House, but the Senate battle remains highly competitive. The scale of Democratic gains in one or both chambers will shape Trump's ability to advance his agenda.

Democratic wins in one or both chambers will likely trigger investigations into ethics of Trump and his administration, their handling of immigration enforcement and the Iran war.

A stronger-than-expected Republican showing could reinforce Trump's grip on the party. Heavy losses could increase pressure to rethink unpopular policies such as tariffs and the war while shaping the message of candidates vying to succeed him.

Early results from Republican-held House seats in Florida and Virginia could provide clues to the size of any Democratic gains. Victories in competitive districts would point to a solid Democratic night, while wins in more Republican-leaning areas could signal a much broader backlash against Trump and his policies.

The close Senate fight will likely hinge on six to eight races. Democrats need to flip several Republican-held seats in states Trump carried by double-digit margins in 2024, including Ohio, Iowa, Alaska and Texas.

Even Kansas, despite Trump's 16-point win there, has become competitive in recent weeks and a Democratic victory would signal a broader wave.

Republicans can retain control by winning most of those contests, while Democrats will likely need to hold Michigan and pick up Maine.

PROBLEMS AT THE POLLS AND VOTE COUNT

Election officials have warned close races could spark disputes over voter eligibility, ballot counting and certification, while long lines, machine malfunctions or challenges by partisan poll watchers could fuel litigation and delay results.

Trump's Justice Department plans to deploy about 1,000 monitors nationwide on Election Day, roughly triple the number used in the last midterms, a move some local officials worry could intimidate voters, although the DOJ says those fears are baseless.

Some election officials and legal experts fear federal investigations and legal challenges could delay or disrupt certification of election results in close races.

On October 22, Trump's Justice Department sued to preemptively block Alaska from certifying the results of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent candidate loses by a narrow margin, saying voters could be confused because two Republicans on the ballot have almost identical names.

Attorney General Todd Blanche on October 22 declined to rule out Justice Department intervention in state election certifications, saying extreme circumstances could warrant action.

Several states are also unlikely to produce complete results on election night, especially in close races, providing fertile ground for disputes.

TRUMP'S RESPONSE TO THE RESULTS

How Trump responds to the results, especially if Republicans lose control of Congress, could become one of the night's biggest stories.

In the early hours of November 4, 2020, before vote counting had finished in several states, Trump declared victory and called for counting to stop.

He ultimately lost to Democrat Joe Biden but continued to falsely claim the election had been stolen, helping fuel the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol by a mob of his supporters who were seeking to stop certification of Biden's win by Congress.

Trump still falsely claims he won the 2020 election and has cast doubt on the integrity of these midterms, raising the prospect of Republican challenges if the party loses one or both chambers.

This year, the Trump administration has pressed states for voter data and launched investigations into noncitizen voting, which election experts and studies have found little evidence to support. It recently sued California over alleged noncitizen ballots.

TURNOUT

Turnout by the parties' core supporters will be important. Opinion polls showed Democrats significantly more enthusiastic about voting than Republicans heading into Election Day.

But strategists caution that Democratic constituencies including young, Black and Hispanic voters have historically turned out at lower rates in midterm elections than in presidential years.

Surveys show persistent skepticism among these groups towards both parties, especially over the cost of living. If turnout among those groups falls short of expectations, Democrats could underperform on Election Day.

Early voting data in states that register voters by party showed higher Democratic engagement. But Republicans argue that many of their supporters traditionally wait until Election Day to vote.

WHAT DO RESULTS MEAN FOR THE 2028 RACE?

After their bruising defeat in the 2024 presidential election, Democrats have been split between those arguing for a more populist economic message and those favoring a centrist approach aimed at winning back swing voters.

Strong performances by moderates and left-wing candidates on Tuesday will allow both factions to claim validation of their policies. That could set the stage for a crowded and potentially contentious contest for the party's 2028 presidential nomination.

DID REPUBLICANS' MONEY ADVANTAGE PAY OFF?

Republicans had a significant financial advantage and flooded the airwaves with ads attacking Democratic candidates.

While some Democrats matched or outraised their opponents, Republicans held an overall spending edge of several hundred million dollars once party committees and outside groups were included.

A key question is whether that advantage helped sway tight races, or whether voter concerns over high prices and the Iran war mattered more.

Trump spent more than $277 million, mostly through his MAGA Inc. super PAC, on a late TV and direct-mail blitz to aid struggling Republican candidates, according to Federal Election Commission data.

Tesla (TSLA.O) CEO Elon Musk spent roughly $366 million during the midterm cycle, including $276 million since July, to support Republican candidates.

Reporting by Tim Reid in Washington, editing by Ross Colvin and Howard Goller

items.title: US senator wants 'full accounting' of Air Force One White House flyover
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 2 (Reuters) - US Senator Tammy Duckworth, the top Democrat on a subcommittee that oversees aviation regulation, asked government agencies on Monday for a full accounting of why they allowed a White House flyover last week by the presidential airplane in what she said was a "dangerous stunt."

The flyover, part of a children's Halloween party attended by President Donald Trump on Thursday, forced a temporary halt to traffic at Reagan Washington National Airport that delayed flights, while city lawmakers voiced concerns that residents, officials and the airport received only 15 minutes' notice.

Duckworth, an Illinois Democrat whose subcommittee oversees the Federal Aviation Administration, said flight-tracking data showed the aircraft made two passes on Thursday over the White House between roughly 400 and 1,000 feet (122 to 305 meters) and close to the top of the Washington Monument.

She said the plane — a Qatari-donated interim presidential aircraft — was below the minimum safe altitude required by the FAA.

"A serious president would be bringing costs down," Duckworth wrote in a letter to the agencies. "This one is busy showing off his toys, putting on full display how wildly out of touch he is with the needs of the American people."

She asked the FAA, the Pentagon and the White House Office of Management and Budget to respond to detailed questions about the cost and limited public notice, while asking the Pentagon if the flight was approved for training and what objective it might have achieved.

Duckworth also asked FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford when the agency was notified and what minimum altitude it authorized.

"The FAA followed all necessary protocols to ensure the safety of Washington, D.C. residents," the White House said, adding the flyover "brought joy and excitement to all those celebrating Halloween at the White House and to many nearby who got to enjoy the spectacle."

Trump is a fan of Air Force One flyovers and they often happen at sporting events he is attending.

The Pentagon and FAA said they would respond directly to Duckworth. The FAA said the flight was coordinated with the agency.

The plane is designated Air Force One when Trump is on board.

The District of Columbia city council said the limited notice of the flyover "startled many, including us."

Airline officials said they had less than an hour's notice.

Some people flying to Washington reported their planes were forced to circle or that they faced delays due to the flyover. FlightAware, a flight-tracking website, said 26% of departing flights and 17% of arriving flights at Reagan National Airport were delayed on Thursday — or 202 in total. Most of those delays were tied to the airport disruption.

Reporting by David Shepardson, Editing by Franklin Paul, Rod Nickel and Edmund Klamann

items.title: US judge dismisses Trump administration's Harvard admissions probe case
items.content_html:
BOSTON, Nov 2 (Reuters) - A federal judge dismissed on Monday a lawsuit by President Donald Trump's administration seeking to force Harvard University to turn over records for an investigation into whether it continues to consider race in its student admissions process.

US District Judge Myong Joun in Boston rejected the US Department of Justice's lawsuit, which Harvard contends was filed as part of a broader campaign by the Republican president's administration against the Ivy League school.

The judge stressed that his decision rested on narrow, procedural grounds and did not resolve whether the Justice Department and US Department of Education could ultimately seek data on thousands of high school students who sought admission at Harvard.

But Joun, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden, agreed with Harvard that the Justice Department sued without taking all legally required steps aimed at securing the university's voluntary compliance with its demands for applicant-level data.

"For example, the complaint does not allege that DOJ informed Harvard of the action it would take — namely, litigation — should Harvard fail to comply, nor does the complaint allege the specific failure identified," Joun wrote.

The Justice Department and Harvard did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Harvard has been a top target of the administration's effort to leverage federal funding and government power to force changes at universities that Trump says are dominated by "radical left" ideologies.

OTHER JUDGES RULED AGAINST ADMINISTRATION

The Cambridge, Massachusetts-based university has already secured rulings from other judges rejecting the administration's efforts to terminate over $2 billion in grants, block the school from hosting international students and sue it for allegedly failing to protect Jewish and Israeli students from harassment.

The Justice Department filed the case before Joun in February, arguing Harvard was not complying with investigations into whether it is following the US Supreme Court's 2023 ruling in a case involving the school rejecting race-conscious admissions programs used to boost enrollment of minority students.

The administration said it needed years of applicant-level admissions data to determine whether race remains a factor in Harvard's admissions decisions and if the university is complying with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which bars racial discrimination in education programs.

Data released by Harvard last week showed Black undergraduate enrollment fell for a third straight year since the Supreme Court barred race-conscious admissions, dropping to 9.3% in the class of 2030 from 11.5% in the class of 2029.

The university's lawyers countered that the case was filed to retaliate against Harvard for refusing demands that it overhaul its governance, hiring and academic programs to align with the administration's agenda.

They said the lawsuit was filed after Trump announced in early February that he was ending settlement talks and wanted $1 billion in damages from Harvard, which he said had "been, for a long time, behaving very badly."

Joun, in dismissing the case on Monday, stressed that he was not resolving whether Harvard has discriminated or if it may ultimately be required to provide data to the agencies. The Justice Department could try to pursue a similar case again if it takes additional administrative steps, he said.

Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani and Rod Nickel

items.title: US judge orders Trump admin to stop demands California remove suspected noncitizen voters
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 2 (Reuters) - A US judge ordered the Trump administration on Monday to stop demanding that California election officials segregate ballots cast by people on its lists of suspected noncitizens.

The ruling by US District Judge James Boasberg comes a day before the November 3 midterm elections, with President Donald Trump's fellow Republicans battling to maintain majorities in both houses of congress.

Boasberg found that the lists the administration had compiled were flawed, and included many people who were wrongly listed as noncitizens.

"California may decide for itself what procedures to use for verifying the citizenship of registered voters," wrote Boasberg, who is based in Washington and was appointed by Democratic President Barack Obama. "The Executive Branch lacks authority to unilaterally impose its preferred procedures.

On Monday, the Supreme Court rejected a bid by the Trump administration to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters who federal officials alleged are likely non-US citizens.

Reporting by Luc Cohen in New York; Editing by Noeleen Walder and Thomas Derpinghaus

items.title: Judge dismisses case against ex-FBI officials, says DOJ rushed charges before midterms
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 2 (Reuters) - A federal judge on Monday tossed out a criminal case accusing two former senior FBI officials of lying about their involvement in an investigation of former President Joe Biden's son Hunter, excoriating the Justice Department for bringing what he said was a political prosecution before Tuesday's midterm elections.

US Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui threw out the case at a remarkably early stage, finding that prosecutors had not shown sufficient evidence that the two officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, both former high-ranking FBI counterintelligence officials, had knowingly made false statements.

"What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization" of federal law enforcement, Faruqui said during a court hearing.

The decision deals another blow to the Justice Department's attempts to investigate people President Donald Trump views as adversaries. It came after a hearing in Washington federal court last week delved into how Trump has exerted control over the DOJ during his second term.

Faruqui, in handing down his decision, assailed the Justice Department for what he described as a rushed investigation that made "critical mistakes" and departed from normal procedures. He suggested that high-ranking officials sought to charge the case last month to influence the midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.

"I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend I cannot read a calendar," Faruqui said in court. "I will not lobotomize myself that way."

A Justice Department spokesperson said the department disagrees with the ruling and is "evaluating all options" to respond.

"The Department's actions will continue to be guided by the facts, the evidence, and the law – not politics," the spokesperson said in a statement.

Prosecutors can seek to revive the case by securing an indictment, but will need approval from a grand jury. Grand juries have declined to approve several high-profile cases during Trump's second term.

Floris broke down in tears and hugged her lawyers and other former high-ranking FBI officials who attended the hearing in support. Kimberly Paschall, a lawyer for Benavides, called the case "an indictment on this current department."

"This so-called prosecution was nothing more than a politically-motivated smear campaign aimed at scoring political points before the midterm elections," Floris' legal team said in a statement following the hearing.

Floris and Benavides were accused of lying during 2023 testimony before the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee about their knowledge of and involvement in probes involving Hunter Biden and material from his personal laptop that surfaced ahead of the 2020 election.

Floris and Benavides both helped supervise an FBI Foreign Influence Task Force that aimed to limit attempts by countries like Russia and China to sway US elections. A criminal complaint said they falsely denied or downplayed their role in certain events involving Hunter Biden, citing internal FBI records and witness interviews.

Faruqui found that some of their statements were not actually false and others could be attributed to "honest mistakes of memory."

An FBI agent testified last week that the probe into Floris and Benavides began with Trump's primetime address in July on election security, during which he announced the FBI would investigate whether US intelligence agencies had suppressed information about Chinese meddling in the 2020 election.

The next day, FBI Director Kash Patel tasked the bureau's Kansas City Field Office with scrutinizing Floris, who had cast doubt on an FBI intelligence report claiming that China sought to interfere in the 2020 election to boost Joe Biden over Trump.

Reporting by Andrew Goudsward, editing by Bhargav Acharya, Chizu Nomiyama and Bill Berkrot

items.title: Judge ends Trump's attempts to sue Wall Street Journal over Epstein reporting
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 31 (Reuters) - (This October 31 story has been republished, with no changes to text.)

President Donald Trump's second attempt to sue the Wall Street Journal was dismissed with prejudice on Saturday, ending his pursuit of a defamation lawsuit over the news outlet's reporting on his ties to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

  • The US District Court for the Southern District of Florida held that Trump again did not show actual malice, a requirement for a public figure's defamation claim. "As with his first attempt, he has failed," Judge Darrin P. Gayles wrote.
  • Gayles highlighted the paper's "thoughtful and detailed investigation" and reporters' efforts to seek comment from Trump and other officials before publishing the article. "Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation," Gayles wrote.
  • Trump's lawyers argued that the story should have been dropped after he denied involvement with Epstein. "That is not what the actual malice standard requires and runs afoul of the First Amendment," Gayles wrote.
  • Trump had refiled the lawsuit seeking at least $10 billion in damages. Saturday's dismissal with prejudice means the case cannot be brought before the court again.

Reporting by Laura Matthews in New York and Jasper Ward in Washington; Editing by Sergio Non and Franklin Paul

items.title: Trump's sweeping makeover of the White House and Washington
items.content_html:
• US president attempts legacy-defining changes to nation's capital
  • Trump's projects face public backlash, preservationist criticism
  • From gold to granite, statues to troops, a city being remade

WASHINGTON, November 2 - President Donald Trump is remaking Washington, recasting the US capital city as a monument to his vision of American greatness with sweeping, unilateral changes his opponents have challenged in court and called a power grab.

Here are some of the projects the real estate entrepreneur-turned-president is pursuing and the challenges they face.

REFLECTING POOL

Trump announced in April that he was remodeling Washington's historic Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, near the site where Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his 1963 "I Have a Dream" speech. Trump said the project would cost up to $2 million.

His administration pursued a more than $16 million renovation on the 2,000-foot (610-meter) pool. Contractors who were not selected through a competitive bidding process worked to finish the project by the July 4 Independence Day holiday.

Trump declared the renovation project complete in June, but the pool soon showed peeling paint and algae growth that turned its crystal-blue waters green. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum defended the original contractor, who was later tasked with repairing the pool.

Trump and other administration officials blamed the damage on vandals, without citing evidence, and authorities arrested a former US Olympic canoeist whom they charged with vandalizing the pool. The former Olympian, David Hearn, denied the charges.

In a court filing, US Attorney Jeanine Pirro and Assistant US Attorney Michael Spence backed away from the case and blamed "a rushed and flawed installation process" instead of Hearn or other accused vandals. Trump said in August that Pirro had "choked" under pressure and "folded like an umbrella."

A judge dismissed the charges in October and ruled that prosecutors could not bring them again.

On Monday, Trump stood before the pool and spoke at length about the renovation in a speech that was billed as his closing argument to voters ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections.

Trump displayed large photos of the algae-infested old pool and spoke at length about the pipes that feed into the water, the grass at the White House, his new Marine One helipad, a golf course, and a triumphal arch facing a court challenge.

"This project should be a project that unites all Americans," he said.

BALLROOM

Trump says a planned 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) White House ballroom will be "the greatest of its kind ever built."

He initially said he and wealthy donors would pay for the estimated $400 million project, but Senate Republicans later unsuccessfully sought $1 billion from Congress that they said would pay for an underground bunker and security features to harden the facility. The White House has not released a full list of the project's donors.

Trump says the new structure will include bomb shelters, medical facilities, defenses against drones and missiles. Facing criticism of the project, his administration now says the facility is needed for national security, an argument the president has also made about a proposed triumphal arch.

The ballroom, which Trump has said will seat 1,000 guests, has faced public backlash. Preservationists and opponents say Trump exceeded his authority by demolishing the historic East Wing, which housed the first lady's offices and the White House movie theater, to make room for the structure.

The US Supreme Court, in a 5-4 ruling in August, allowed Trump to continue construction while he challenges a judicial order that would halt much of the development. In a dissent, Chief Justice John Roberts said the project was "likely unlawful."

KENNEDY CENTER

Congress created the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts to honor the Democratic president, who was assassinated in 1963. The marble-walled facility sits alongside the Potomac River and hosts concerts, plays and an annual awards gala that has presented lifetime achievement honors to celebrities like Robert Redford, Cher and Stevie Wonder.

Since taking office in 2025, Trump has purged the center's leadership, changed its programming and appointed a board that added his name to the edifice. Trump has repeatedly said his name should be on the building in exchange for his work raising money to renovate the facility.

But a US district court judge ordered in May that the Kennedy Center remove his name. The Kennedy Center board subsequently voted on a new plan to put Trump's name back on the building. A judge rejected that plan in September, and the board decided the same day to shut down the venue for up to two years for repairs and an at least $257 million renovation project.

Trump later refused to say whether he would attempt to demolish the facility. Litigation continues. Meanwhile, December's Kennedy Center Honors will be held at Washington's Capital One Arena.

Other cultural centers in Washington have also been in focus, including the city's Smithsonian museums. In July, Trump signed an executive order ordering the installation of temporary signage in front of the National Museum of American History correcting "inaccurate information presented in the Museum." The order said the museum "failed to appropriately honor the 56 signers of the Declaration of Independence."

WHITE HOUSE GROUNDS

Trump has transformed the historic Oval Office with gold accents and statuettes, portraits of famous Americans pulled from storage and a copy of the Declaration of Independence that hangs on the wall.

Outside the Oval Office, Trump replaced the Rose Garden's grass lawn with a white stone patio and umbrella-covered tables, evoking Trump's Mar-a-Lago Club in Palm Beach, Florida.

Trump also added statues of US independence heroes Alexander Hamilton and Benjamin Franklin in the garden, along with a sculpture called "Freedom's Charge" that depicts two Revolutionary War soldiers.

Trump ripped out the flagstone walkway that had lined the West Wing colonnade adjacent to the Rose Garden for 60 years and replaced it with black granite.

Along the colonnade wall, he placed portraits of America's past presidents, with a plaque beneath each inscribed with Trump's view of that person. Trump did not include a portrait of Joe Biden, who defeated him in the 2020 election.

He also built a multimillion-dollar granite helipad on the White House South Lawn to protect the grass from the exhaust of the latest Marine One helicopter.

The South Lawn was redesigned after Trump hosted an Ultimate Fighting Championship event there in June.

Trump has also worked to renovate Lafayette Square, a public park in front of the White House, which has been largely closed to the public in 2026.

TRIUMPHAL ARCH

Across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial lies a highway roundabout near the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery where Trump wants to build a "triumphal arch."

The arch would resemble the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, but dwarf the Parisian landmark. Trump has said the arch would double as a "military complex" housing drones and snipers.

The arch, with eagle statues and a Lady Liberty-type figure on top, would be about 250 feet (76 meters) tall. That is taller than the Lincoln Memorial and close to the height of the US Capitol, which, at 288 feet, can be seen across much of Washington. The site is near airplanes' final approach to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

Veterans have sued to block the arch, arguing it would destroy the historic sight line between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

EAST POTOMAC GOLF LINKS

The president is working to overhaul Washington's East Potomac Golf Links, a century-old public golf course. Trump, a frequent golfer who owns several courses, has said he hopes the renovation will allow the course to host major tournaments.

That project is also tied up in legal challenges by groups that say it violates the law that created the park. It's not clear what would remain of the park's public space under a redesign of the golf course.

Sixty-one Democratic lawmakers raised concerns in June that "over 35,000 cubic yards of toxic debris left over from the demolition of the former East Wing" were placed on the golf course.

A report prepared for the National Park Service by a Virginia engineering firm in April identified some toxic metals and other contaminants in the debris. The Interior Department, which oversees the National Park Service, said the project met all legal standards.

GARDEN OF AMERICAN HEROES

Trump has talked about establishing a National Garden of American Heroes since his first term in office in 2017-2021. Congress provided $40 million for the project in 2025, which Trump plans to develop at West Potomac Park along the Potomac River to mark the 250th anniversary of US independence.

Trump said the park will include statues of the country's founding fathers, military members, religious leaders, civil rights champions, athletes, and artists and entertainers.

Preservation groups have sued to have the project halted on legal grounds.

STREETS OF WASHINGTON

As part of a slate of moves in Washington, Trump has deployed thousands of National Guard troops to the capital city as the centerpiece of what he describes as a no-holds-barred effort to combat crime, especially in Democratic-led cities.

Every day, small groups of soldiers in camouflage and body armor patrol tourist-heavy areas of the US capital, including national monuments, subway stations and the area around its professional baseball park.

It's unclear how much police work the troops have done. A Reuters analysis in August found that in the first year since their arrival, the National Guard troops have been mentioned in only a tiny fraction — about 1.3% — of the criminal cases filed in the Superior Court of the District of Columbia, which handles nearly all the city's criminal prosecutions. In dozens of cases, the soldiers appear not as people making the arrests but as victims of crime.

Local police said overall crime in the city declined by 18% in 2025 and by another 11% during the year through November 2, though violent crime rose by 12% in 2026.

Reporting By Steve Holland and Trevor Hunnicutt, editing by Deepa Babington and Sanjeev Miglani

items.title: US manufacturing strengthens in October, input prices stay high
items.content_html:
• Manufacturing PMI increases one point to 55.5 in October
  • Prices paid by factories for inputs remain elevated
  • Supplier deliveries slowed for an 11th straight month amid shortages of metals and chips

WASHINGTON, Nov 2 (Reuters) - US manufacturing activity picked up in October amid strong domestic demand, keeping inflation at the factory gate elevated.

Despite the unexpected improvement reported by the Institute for Supply Management on Monday, sentiment among manufacturers remained overwhelmingly downbeat, with some complaining that "economic policies coming out of Washington continue to weigh on business conditions," and others saying the situation was "making it impossible to make sound long-term decisions."

They were likely referring to rising prices for a range of commodities including energy, stemming from the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran. A recent escalation in the trade war with Canada was also cited by manufacturers as a constraint.

The inflation fallout from the Middle East conflict has also helped depress consumer sentiment, culminating in broad disapproval of President Donald Trump's stewardship of the economy. Discontent over the rising cost of living is likely to determine control of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections.

Economists cautioned that rising interest rates and declining inflation-adjusted household income would hamper manufacturing activity next year, especially the segments not exposed to the artificial intelligence spending frenzy.

"While AI-related investment is expected to remain strong, further shifts in AI sentiment, which has worsened in recent weeks, could weigh on investment plans," said Veronica Clark, an economist at Citigroup. "Even if current investment plans proceed, this would still suggest a slowing growth rate of future investment. Additionally, higher rates and recently tighter financial conditions could weigh on non-AI related parts of the manufacturing sector."

The ISM said its manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index increased to 55.5 last month from 54.5 in September. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the PMI would stay at 54.5. The PMI has stayed above the 50 threshold this year, indicating growth in manufacturing, a sector that accounts for about 9.4% of the economy.

A measure of production at factories jumped 2.3 percentage points to 59 last month, the highest reading since November 2021.

Twelve industries reported growth, including transportation equipment, electrical equipment, appliances and components, machinery, primary metals, textile mills, and computer and electronic products. The three industries reporting a contraction were paper products, printing and related support activities, and nonmetallic mineral products.

Activity is being driven by robust consumer spending and business spending on AI. The government reported last week that domestic demand grew at its fastest pace in more than five years in the third quarter.

The overall economy grew at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter after expanding at a 2.2% pace in the April-June period, even as the war in the Middle East stoked inflation. The ISM survey's new orders measure edged up to 55.5 from 55.3 in September, with exports also rising.

Factory inventories also increased. The government's advance GDP report showed that business inventories rebounded last quarter after having been drawn down for five straight quarters.

SENTIMENT CONTINUES TO DETERIORATE

Still, Susan Spence, who chairs the ISM Manufacturing Business Survey Committee, noted that "general sentiment got worse for a third month in a row." She reported that 66% of commentary from respondents was negative, with pricing volatility dominating the downbeat views, followed by longer lead times, tariffs and the war.

Some makers of fabricated metal products said "customers are unwilling to make commitments to anything other than the shortest term due to the vast uncertainty." Their counterparts in the chemical products industry said "negative, inflation, in the red are the three words or phrases that best describe our strategic sourcing for 2026."

Some manufacturers of transportation equipment said "customers continue to be in a wait-and-see mode," adding that they "continue to be gobsmacked by the high price of equipment when they ask for quotes." The AI race and construction of data centers are also putting a strain on supply and boosting prices.

"Any commodity consumed by AI/data centers is in a crunch, both for supply and pricing," said some businesses in the miscellaneous manufacturing sector. Machinery manufacturers reported that "explosive growth in the semiconductor and government/defense spaces has put us on our heels as we try to work through demand."

The survey's supplier deliveries index inched up to 59.1 from 59.0 in September. A reading above 50 indicates slower deliveries. Suppliers' delivery performance to manufacturing organizations slowed for the 11th straight month.

Among the products that remained in short supply were aluminum, copper, electrical and electronic components, and memory chips. Strained supply chains meant factories continued to pay more for inputs.

The survey's gauge of prices paid for inputs eased to a still-high 75.2 from 77.9 in September, supporting economists' views that inflation will continue to run above the Federal Reserve's 2% target into 2027. Prices continued to rise for a number of products, including aluminum, copper, diesel fuel, and electronic and memory components.

The government last week reported that the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index rose 3.6% year over year in September. It is one of the inflation measures monitored by the US central bank for monetary policy.

The Fed last Wednesday left its benchmark overnight interest rate within the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated." Economists expect the US central bank to raise borrowing costs in December.

Factory employment continued to grow last month, though the pace slowed from September. A measure of employment in the sector edged down to 52.4 from 52.7 in September, slightly above economists' forecast of 52.0.

"Persistent supply constraints and elevated input costs suggest the inflationary blaze remains far from contained," said Priscilla Thiagamoorthy, a senior economist at BMO Capital Markets. "The combination of firmer factory activity and still-hot prices is not a good mix for the Fed."

items.title: Tensions rise as midterm campaign ends with control of Congress at stake
items.content_html:
DETROIT/WASHINGTON, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Congressional candidates and President Donald Trump made their final arguments to US voters on Monday, the eve of the midterm elections, with tensions running high in Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed aims to become the first Muslim elected to the Senate.

California was also in the spotlight after the Supreme Court swiftly quashed an attempt by Trump's Justice Department to intervene and block vote counting from alleged non-US citizens.

With control of the US Congress at stake for his final two years in office, Trump devoted his last major speech before voting day to touting renovations of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, one of the Washington public works projects he has made a priority since returning to the White House.

He later spoke by telephone on Fox News' "Hannity" show, urging Republicans to pretend he is on the ballot in an effort to increase voter participation.

"We have to vote. If our people vote, we win in a landslide," Trump said.

All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 US Senate seats will be contested on Tuesday. Democrats are widely favored to retake the House but face a greater challenge in the Senate.

Loss of control in either chamber would constrain Trump and empower Democrats to investigate his administration, while a Senate majority would also allow them to block his appointees to federal courts including the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Trump administration's attempt to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters who federal officials alleged were likely non-US citizens.

It was quick action from the high court. California had argued the federal lawsuit would disenfranchise 20,000 voters based on vague accusations and that the process for identifying noncitizens was error-prone.

A US judge on Monday also ordered the Trump administration to stop demanding that California segregate ballots cast by people on lists of suspected noncitizens.

Trump, 80, has campaigned hard for Republicans, holding events in 20 states over the past 32 days, the White House said. His final in-person event was a speech at the belated reopening of the Washington reflecting pool, where the former real-estate developer spent more than 20 minutes discussing pipes, joints, caulking, granite resurfacing, algae and leaks.

"So we have a lot of great things planned for Washington, and I could get into the nation, but for that you don't have enough time," Trump said, also mentioning the grass at the White House, his new Marine One helipad, a golf course and plans for a triumphal arch that are facing a court challenge.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday found 46% of registered voters said they would vote for Democrats in congressional elections, compared with 38% who picked Republicans.

Early voting, whether in person or by mail, has already set a record with 57 million votes cast as of Monday afternoon, up from 45 million in all of the 2022 midterms, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab.

MICHIGAN TENSIONS HIGH

In Michigan, Democratic candidate El-Sayed, a physician and former public health official, is attempting to become the first Muslim elected to the Senate, running against Republican Mike Rogers.

Their tight Senate race grew more heated over the weekend when US Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed, switched to backing Rogers.

Afterward, El-Sayed's campaign said it raised $2.4 million on Sunday, its largest single-day fundraising haul, fueled by small-dollar donations.

El-Sayed, an Egyptian American Muslim born in Michigan, has been targeted by Trump and other Republicans who have questioned his loyalty to the US and baselessly called him a terrorist sympathizer. El-Sayed has called questions about his loyalty to the US "shameful."

On Fox News' "Hannity" show on Monday Rogers cast El-Sayed as "just too extreme."

At a Michigan rally on Monday, Rogers said, "This election was never about how someone prayed. It was always about how you think, what your philosophy and what your ideology is."

El-Sayed appealed for unity at a campaign rally on Monday, saying, "I believe that we have the opportunity to breach those divides, divides of geography, of race, of sexual orientation, gender identity, of faith, to build together what we only can have together."

TRUMP SEEKS TO INTERVENE

The Trump administration also has sought to intervene in election disputes in Alaska.

A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a US Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification of election results in Alaska if Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan narrowly loses. The Justice Department has argued voters may be confused by a challenger named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the same ballot.

The issue of two Sullivans running in Alaska has roiled the campaign since the New York Times reported last week that Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting the latter Sullivan into the race as a spoiler.

The senator said on Sunday he would accept the results of Tuesday's election even as the Trump administration presses a criminal investigation into the issue.

Peltola has denied involvement, and Sullivan Jr. has denied coordinating with Peltola's campaign.

Introduced as "the real Dan Sullivan" at a rally in Alaska on Monday, the senator said Democrats see Alaska as key to taking control of the Senate.

"It's not just about Alaska," he said. "We are the firewall for freedom for America right now."

A supporter of the Senate challenger Sullivan Jr. said FBI agents on Friday questioned him about his $500 donation. Barry Bracken, a retired fisheries biologist living in Sullivan's hometown of Petersburg, Alaska, where he said they have known each other more than 40 years, said he told the agents he had intentionally donated to Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.'s campaign, and they left soon after.

The FBI did not reply to a request for comment.

items.title: Six reasons Democrats may fall short of a midterm landslide
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, November 2 - Republican President Donald Trump's low approval ratings, voter concern over high prices and dissatisfaction with the Iran war have led many analysts and opinion polls to predict significant Democratic gains in Tuesday's midterm elections.

But six analysts and party strategists told Reuters several factors could prevent Democrats from turning those favorable political conditions into a landslide, even if the party ultimately makes gains in Congress.

Recent opinion polls have shown Democrats increasingly competitive in once reliably Republican seats and the party has been expanding its efforts into Trump's conservative heartland.

Democrats are widely expected to have a good election night, but the scale of any victory is still uncertain.

Here are six reasons Democrats may fall short of expectations.

FEWER COMPETITIVE HOUSE RACES

The number of competitive US House races has shrunk sharply over the past three decades as partisan polarization and redistricting – including gerrymandering – have made more seats safely Democratic or Republican.

As a result, analysts estimate that only about 40 to 50 of the House's 435 seats are truly competitive this year.

Most expect Democrats to retake the lower chamber from Republicans, but with a majority of perhaps 5 to 20 seats, limiting the scope for gains like those in 2018, when Democrats picked up 41 seats.

Bill Galston, a former White House adviser to President Bill Clinton, said if Democrats gain even 25 House seats, "they'd have a working majority, but not a huge one."

Such a majority would give Democrats control of the House but little room to maneuver, making it harder to pass contentious legislation or claim the sweeping mandate associated with past wave elections.

SENATE MAJORITY NO SURE THING

While Democrats are favored to make gains in the 100-member Senate, achieving the net gain of four seats needed for a 51-49 majority remains far from certain because many of their top pickup targets are in states Trump carried by wide margins in 2024.

David Wasserman, an elections analyst at the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, said Democrats must make breakthroughs in states Trump carried by double digits. Even a national swing of 10 percentage points toward Democrats would likely leave the party two seats short of a majority, he said.

Democrats also face tougher-than-expected contests in states they had hoped would be safer, including Maine, New Hampshire and Michigan.

"Republicans are hanging very close in those races," said Andrew Busch, a public policy professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and author of a history of midterm elections.

"That's not necessarily what you would expect if things were going well for Democrats across the board."

TURNOUT

Opinion polls show Democratic voters more enthusiastic than Republicans, but strategists caution that such Democratic constituencies as young, Black and Hispanic voters have historically turned out at lower rates in midterm elections than in presidential years.

Surveys show persistent skepticism among these groups towards both parties, especially over the cost of living. If turnout among those groups falls short of expectations, Democrats could underperform on Election Day, analysts said.

Early voting data in states that register voters by party showed higher Democratic engagement. But Republicans argue that many of their supporters traditionally wait until Election Day to vote.

In the 2022 midterms, voters aged 50 and older made up nearly twice as much of the electorate as those under 50. In recent years older voters have leaned Republican, according to exit-poll surveys.

REPUBLICAN MONEY ADVANTAGE

Republicans entered the campaign's final stretch with a substantial financial advantage, although spending in key races so far has had mixed results.

Republicans held a cash advantage of several hundred million dollars heading into the final weeks of the campaign across their national party committees and major allied super PACs, according to committee filings and Federal Election Commission data.

Trump spent more than $277 million, mostly through his MAGA Inc. super PAC, on a late TV and direct-mail blitz to aid struggling Republican candidates, according to Federal Election Commission data.

Tesla (TSLA.O) CEO Elon Musk spent roughly $366 million during the midterm cycle, including $276 million since July, to support Republican candidates.

Republicans outspent Democrats by $188 million in Senate battleground advertising by the end of September, according to AdImpact, which tracks advertising spending.

"Any time you have one side with a big financial advantage and the ability to pour it into races at the last minute, it can tip the result of close races," Busch said.

POLLS HAVE MISSED REPUBLICAN STRENGTH

Opinion polls have frequently underestimated Republican support in recent election cycles. Reuters/Ipsos polling shows registered voters favoring Democrats over Republicans by 47% to 35% on the congressional generic ballot.

The largest polling misses came when Trump was on the ballot. Trump, who is not on the ballot this year, has urged supporters to treat November's election as if he were.

Polls significantly understated Republican strength in the 2014 midterms, when the party won a sweeping Senate victory. But midterm polls in 2022 underestimated how well Democrats would perform.

SOCIALISM ATTACKS COULD RESONATE

Trump and many Republican candidates have sought to paint Democrats as socialists and extremists who pose an existential threat to the country.

Democrats in competitive races are increasingly declaring themselves proud capitalists, worried that the Republican tactics could sway critical independent voters.

Republicans are highlighting victories by members of the Democratic Socialists of America movement and progressive candidates in Democratic primaries to portray the whole party as socialist, even though fewer than two dozen of them scored wins this year.

Galston said the attacks could resonate with some wavering voters and influence close races.

"It might be effective at the margins," Galston said. "It could reduce the Democratic advantage by one or two points in the close races."

Reporting by Tim Reid in Washington. Additional reporting by Dawn Kopecki. Editing by Ross Colvin, Howard Goller and Alistair Bell

items.title: US judge dismisses Trump election lawsuit in Alaska
items.content_html:
Nov 1 (Reuters) - A federal judge on Sunday threw out a lawsuit by President Donald Trump's administration seeking to block Alaska from certifying a loss by Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in Tuesday's midterm elections if votes for a rival who shares his name could have changed the outcome.

The ruling by US District Judge Sharon Gleason in Anchorage was the latest blow to Trump's efforts to assert a greater federal role in elections, which under the US Constitution are administered by the states.

Democratic former US Representative Mary Peltola is challenging Sullivan in the race, whose outcome could prove critical for determining whether Trump's fellow Republicans can retain control of the Senate in the midterms. Democrats need a net gain of at least four seats in November's midterm elections to gain control of the Senate.

Alaska's ballot features the names of the incumbent senator, Daniel S. Sullivan, and Peltola, as well as a retired teacher whose name is Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., and another long-shot candidate.

Peltola has denied involvement in any effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan, who lives in a remote fishing village, to enter the race, saying at a rally that she is "not interested in tricking voters." The retired teacher has denied in interviews with US news outlets that his aim is to cause confusion, but has said he would prefer Peltola winning over the incumbent senator.

In her decision, Gleason wrote that the administration's proposal to segregate ballots would violate the right of voters in Alaska to a secret ballot, and dismissed the case on the basis that the federal government lacked the necessary legal standing to bring it.

"The United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy," Gleason wrote, referring to the Trump administration's lawsuit.

The Justice Department said in a court filing it intends to appeal the ruling. In a statement, it said the judge's order dismissing the lawsuit was on procedural grounds. Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled "in an attempt to rig outcomes," the Justice Department said.

Alaska's elections division welcomed the ruling, saying it rejected a last-minute administration effort to intervene in the election and allows the state to focus on administering a fair vote while protecting ballot secrecy.

The American Civil Liberties Union, which intervened in the lawsuit in support of Alaska, said the judge rebuffed a Justice Department effort to "throw out Alaska's election results before a single ballot was counted."

"This administration keeps trying to tilt the midterms, and today (Sunday) it lost again," the ACLU said.

ELECTION OVERSIGHT

The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the moves as federal overreach.

The lawsuit filed by the Justice Department on October 22 challenged the candidacy of the retired teacher. According to the lawsuit, he is running "with the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan into voting for him." The administration said that certifying the election could violate the federal government's duty to protect the integrity of elections.

The suit sought to temporarily bar Alaska election officials from certifying a Peltola victory in the event that assigning all of Daniel J. Sullivan's votes to the incumbent would have changed the results. The lawsuit said that, in such a scenario, Gleason should investigate whether voters who selected Daniel J. Sullivan had instead intended to support the incumbent.

'BALLOT STACKING'

The New York Times reported on October 28 that Peltola campaign staff members had worked with a Democratic operative from Ohio to find another Dan Sullivan to run to peel votes from the Republican senator. Reuters has not verified the report.

It is not clear what, if any, laws may have been broken. Both parties have engaged in "ballot stacking" by propping up lesser-known candidates to siphon votes from their opponents.

Trump, who has told reporters he ordered the Justice Department to file the lawsuit, has called for Peltola to be criminally prosecuted. The Justice Department has brought criminal charges against a number of Trump's adversaries.

Peltola's campaign had called the lawsuit meritless.

items.title: Democratic Senator Murphy hospitalized after stroke, chief of staff says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 1 (Reuters) - Democratic US Senator Chris Murphy was hospitalized after suffering a stroke, the senator's chief of staff said on Sunday.

Murphy began experienceing numbness in his arm while attending his son's hockey game on Saturday afternoon, said Allison Herwitt, chief of staff to the Connecticut senator.

"He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke. He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment," she said in a statement.

"The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery."

Reporting by Doina Chiacu; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama
